raw_case_text:
A 26-year-old male with a history of subtotal colectomy and ileostomy for an inflammatory pelvic mass was referred to our unit for further assessment. He had no other medical comorbidities and had good exercise tolerance. Assessment with contrast enhanced computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging showed resolution of the inflammatory mass, and a decision was made to restore the bowel continuity. Six months following the initial surgery, he underwent excision of the rectal stump (as it was found to be fibrotic) followed by an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis.
On the second postoperative day, he developed respiratory distress, tachycardia, and fever. Inflammatory markers were elevated with a white blood cell count (WBC) of 22 x 109/l. Arterial blood gas showed a type 1 respiratory failure. A computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram was performed suspecting a pulmonary embolism which was negative. However, there was bilateral basal consolidation. He improved with supportive care with resolution of fever within 24 hours.
Thereafter, his recovery was uneventful till day 5 with a functioning ileostomy and the abdominal drain was removed on day 4. On day 6, he had continuous bleeding from the drain site. On day 7, he again developed respiratory distress with a drop in saturation to 88% on air. There was drain-site oozing. He had no fever, and the haemodynamic parameters including urine output were normal. His full blood count revealed severe thrombocytopenia and haemoconcentration (WBC: 4.4, haemoglobin: 24.2 g/dl, haematocrit: 67.8, and platelet: 9), and C-reactive protein was 290 mg/dl (Figures 1 and 2). His liver enzymes were mildly elevated and renal functions were normal. His abdomen was nontender, and ileostomy was functioning normally. Ultrasound scan showed bilateral moderate-to-massive pleural effusion and moderate ascites. A right intercostal tube was inserted, and he was transferred to the ICU for intensive monitoring. The dengue IgM and IgG were positive. He was managed for dengue haemorrhagic fever and bilateral lower zone pneumonia with intravenous antibiotics, targeted fluid therapy, supportive care, and monitoring. Platelet transfusion was given as he had persistent drain-site oozing. He improved with supportive care. The drain site oozing seized after 48 hours, and the intercostal tube was removed on day 11. Thereafter, his recovery was uneventful and was discharged (Figure 3). Informed written consent was obtained from the patient prior to collection of data for publication.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old male presenting with postoperative drain-site bleeding, respiratory distress, and oxygen desaturation seven days after ileal pouch-anal anastomosis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 26-year-old male underwent elective excision of rectal stump and ileal pouch-anal anastomosis 6 months after subtotal colectomy and ileostomy. On postoperative day 2, he developed transient fever, tachycardia, and type 1 respiratory failure that improved within 24 hours. The abdominal drain was removed on day 4. On day 6, continuous bleeding occurred from the drain site. On day 7, he re-developed acute respiratory distress with SpO2 dropping to 88% on room air and persistent drain-site oozing, necessitating urgent thoracostomy tube placement and transfer to the intensive care unit.
subjective.past_medical_history: Subtotal colectomy and ileostomy for an inflammatory pelvic mass 6 months prior; no other medical comorbidities; good baseline exercise tolerance.
subjective.review_of_systems: Functioning ileostomy; absence of abdominal pain; absence of fever at time of secondary deterioration.

objective.physical_examination: Postoperative day 7: Afebrile, respiratory distress with oxygen saturation 88% on room air, hemodynamic parameters stable, urine output normal. Abdomen soft, non-tender; persistent oozing from the abdominal drain site; ileostomy functioning normally.
objective.routine_investigations: Postoperative day 2 labs: WBC 22 x 10^9/L; ABG showed type 1 respiratory failure. Postoperative day 7 labs: WBC 4.4 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin 24.2 g/dL, hematocrit 67.8% (severe hemoconcentration), platelet count 9 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 290 mg/dL; liver enzymes mildly elevated; renal functions normal. Abdominal and thoracic ultrasound: Bilateral moderate-to-massive pleural effusion and moderate ascites.
objective.advanced_workup: Preoperative imaging: Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI showed resolution of inflammatory pelvic mass. Postoperative day 2 CT pulmonary angiogram: Negative for pulmonary embolism; demonstrated bilateral basal consolidation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection (dengue hemorrhagic fever with severe plasma leakage, hemoconcentration, marked thrombocytopenia, and surgical drain bleeding) complicated by bilateral lower zone pneumonia in the early postoperative period. Confirmed by positive Dengue serology (IgM and IgG positive). Pulmonary embolism was ruled out by CT pulmonary angiogram.
Plan & Outcome: Transferred to the ICU for intensive hemodynamic and respiratory monitoring. Managed with right intercostal chest tube insertion, targeted intravenous fluid therapy, platelet transfusions for persistent drain-site bleeding, intravenous antibiotics for bilateral pneumonia, and supportive care. Drain-site oozing ceased within 48 hours; intercostal tube was removed on postoperative day 11. The patient made a complete recovery and was discharged home.
